Loading data¶

I start from the processed endothelial-cell object. I am not reprocessing the raw data here. For this project I only want to inspect the published annotations, metadata, and marker patterns.

In [62]:
#checking if data file exists
data = sc.read_h5ad(data_path)
print(data)

#checking data dimensions
print("Cells:", data.n_obs)
print("Genes:", data.n_vars)

Metadata and annotation columns¶

The object is already filtered to endothelial cells, so I use the existing annotations provided with the dataset.

For this analysis, I use:

  • organ_uni as the organ/tissue label
  • art_ven as the broad endothelial compartment label
  • cap as the capillary-related label
  • ann_ec_states as the endothelial-state annotation
  • donor, sample_id, study, and dataset to keep track of where cells come from

Cell counts by organ and annotation¶

I first count how many cells are present for each organ and annotation label. These counts describe the dataset, not the real abundance of endothelial cells in the body.

In [68]:
cell_counts_by_organ = (
    data.obs[organ_col]
    .value_counts(dropna=False)
    .rename_axis("organ")
    .reset_index(name="n_cells"))

cell_counts_by_broad_state = (
    data.obs[broad_state_col]
    .value_counts(dropna=False)

The dataset is not evenly distributed across organs or annotation labels. This matters because large groups can dominate later visualizations, especially UMAPs and summary plots.

UMAP overview¶

The dataset already includes UMAP coordinates, so I use them to look at the existing annotations on the processed object.

In [72]:
#listing embeddings
list(data.obsm.keys())

#plotting umap colored by organ
sc.pl.umap(data,
    color=organ_col,
    frameon=False,
    title="Organ")

#plotting umap colored by broad state
sc.pl.umap(data,
        color=broad_state_col,
        frameon=False,
        title="Broad state")

#plotting umap colored by cap
sc.pl.umap(data,
        color=cap_col,
        frameon=False,
        title="Cap label")
In [73]:
#plot umap by dataset (batch effect)
sc.pl.umap(
    data,
    color=dataset_col,
    frameon=False,
    title="Dataset")

#plot umap by study (batch effect)
sc.pl.umap(
    data,
    color=study_col,
    frameon=False,
    title="Study"
)

These UMAPs are only a first visual check. I use them to see how organs, annotations, and source datasets are arranged in the processed object.

The dataset and study labels are mixed across much of the UMAP, although some regions are still enriched for specific sources. So I would not say the embedding is obviously dominated by dataset source, but I also cannot use a UMAP to rule out batch effects.

15 rows × 24 columns

The cap and ann_ec_states columns are closely related. Many labels match directly. The main difference is that cap groups arterial and venous cells more broadly, while ann_ec_states keeps more detailed arterial and venous subtypes.

For the next plots, I use cap because it is detailed enough to show tissue-related endothelial labels, but not as fragmented as ann_ec_states.

Marker checks¶

I next check a small set of known vascular markers across the existing labels. I am not re-annotating the cells here; I just want to see whether the labels behave as expected.

In [77]:
#building marker dict
marker_genes = {
    "pan_endothelial": ["PECAM1", "CDH5", "VWF", "KDR"],
    "arterial": ["GJA5", "SOX17", "EFNB2", "DLL4"],
    "venous": ["NR2F2", "ACKR1"],
    "capillary": ["RGCC", "CA4", "EMCN", "PLVAP"],
    "lung_capillary": ["EDNRB", "SOSTDC1"],
    "blood_brain_barrier": ["CLDN5", "SLC2A1", "ABCB1"],
    "liver_zonation": ["RAMP3", "CLEC4G"],
    "kidney_glomerular": ["EHD3", "PLVAP"]}

#checking which genes are present
all_markers = [gene
    for genes in marker_genes.values()
    for gene in genes]

marker_presence = pd.DataFrame({"gene": all_markers,
    "present_in_object": [gene in data.var_names for gene in all_markers]})

print(marker_presence)

#keep present genes
present_markers = marker_presence.loc[marker_presence["present_in_object"],
    "gene"].tolist()

print(present_markers)

    data,
    var_names=present_markers,
    groupby=cap_col,

The marker plot mostly behaves as expected. Pan-endothelial markers are present across most groups, arterial markers are strongest in art_ec, venous markers are strongest in ven_ec, and blood-brain-barrier markers are strongest in blood_brain_barrier_ec.

I use this as a marker check, not as a new annotation.

#plotting results
from plotnine import geom_tile, scale_fill_gradient, element_text

organ_cap_long = (organ_cap_pct
    .reset_index()
    .melt(
        id_vars=organ_col,
        var_name="cap_label",
        value_name="pct_cells"
    ))

(ggplot(
        organ_cap_long,
        aes(x="cap_label", y=organ_col, fill="pct_cells")
    )
    + geom_tile()
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="white", high="red")
    + labs(
        x="Endothelial label",
        y="Organ",
        fill="% cells",
        title="Endothelial labels by organ"
    )
    + theme_bw()
    + theme(
        axis_text_x=element_text(rotation=45, ha="right")
    ))
Out[80]:

The heatmap separates broad labels from more tissue-associated labels. art_ec, ven_ec, and cap_ec appear across several organs, while labels such as blood_brain_barrier_ec, glomeruli_ec, aerocyte_ec, and liver capillary labels are mostly tied to specific organs.

This should not be read as real endothelial abundance across organs. It only describes what is present in this processed object.

Clustering sensitivity check¶

Single-cell clusters are not fixed objects. Here I run a small Leiden clustering check using the stored scVI embedding and vary a few basic parameters.

In [81]:

sc.tl.leiden( data,
    resolution=0.5,
    key_added="leiden_r05_n15")

As expected, higher Leiden resolution gives more clusters. The match to the existing cap labels is moderate, not perfect.

The best match in this small grid is at n_neighbors = 30 and resolution = 0.3. At higher resolution, Leiden starts splitting the data into more clusters, and the agreement with the existing labels drops.

This is enough for the point I wanted to check: clustering recovers part of the annotation structure, but the exact clusters depend on the parameters. I keep the published labels as the reference.

In [87]:
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, normalized_mutual_info_score

sensitivity_results = []

for n_neighbors in [15, 30]:
    sc.pp.neighbors(
        data,
        use_rep="X_scVI",
        n_neighbors=n_neighbors,
        key_added=f"neighbors_n{n_neighbors}")
    
    for resolution in [0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0]:
        cluster_key = f"leiden_r{str(resolution).replace('.', '')}_n{n_neighbors}"
        
        sc.tl.leiden(data,
            resolution=resolution,
            neighbors_key=f"neighbors_n{n_neighbors}",
            key_added=cluster_key)
        
        ari = adjusted_rand_score(
            data.obs[cap_col].astype(str),
            data.obs[cluster_key].astype(str))
        
        nmi = normalized_mutual_info_score(
            data.obs[cap_col].astype(str),
            data.obs[cluster_key].astype(str))
        
        n_clusters = data.obs[cluster_key].nunique()
        
        sensitivity_results.append({
            "n_neighbors": n_neighbors,
            "resolution": resolution,
            "cluster_key": cluster_key,
            "n_clusters": n_clusters,
            "ARI_vs_cap": ari,
            "NMI_vs_cap": nmi
        })

sensitivity_results = pd.DataFrame(sensitivity_results)
sensitivity_results

Out[89]:

Increasing the Leiden resolution increases the number of clusters, as expected. The similarity to the existing cap labels is moderate across settings: the clustering recovers part of the published annotation structure, but it does not reproduce it exactly.

The highest similarity is observed with a lower-resolution setting (n_neighbors = 30, resolution = 0.3). At higher resolution, Leiden produces more clusters and the match to the existing labels decreases, which suggests that finer clustering begins to split published labels into smaller groups.

NMI remains around 0.68–0.74, again suggesting partial but not exact agreement between simple clustering and the existing labels.

Overall, this check supports a cautious use of clustering. A simple Leiden workflow on the stored scVI embedding captures several major endothelial groups, but the exact cluster boundaries depend on parameter choices. For this reason, I keep the published annotations as the main reference and use clustering only as a secondary check.

Notes from this analysis¶

This is a small analysis on a processed object, so I do not use it to claim new endothelial states or subpopulations.

The existing labels are understandable from the data. Arterial, venous, capillary, and some tissue-associated labels show up in the UMAPs, in the marker plot, and in the organ-label heatmap.

The organ-label heatmap was the most useful summary for me. It shows the difference between broad labels such as art_ec, ven_ec, and cap_ec, and labels that are mostly tied to one organ or tissue type, such as blood_brain_barrier_ec, glomeruli_ec, aerocyte_ec, and liver capillary labels.

The clustering check also helped. A simple Leiden clustering recovers part of the existing annotation structure, but the result changes when resolution and neighborhood size change. So I keep the published labels as the reference and use clustering only as a check.
